quote: A journalist asked Einstein what he would do if Eddington’s observations failed to match his theory.
content: Conceded: the quotation comes from Rosenthal-Schneider, and it was spoken after the telegram arrived. The essay's argument does not depend on when it was said. Its question is whether Einstein was entitled to his confidence before the eclipse. The record of November 1915, when the new field equations produced the 43 arcseconds of Mercury's anomalous perihelion that the Entwurf theory could not, shows the observational evidence already in hand (Janssen 2005). A counterfactual stated after the fact still describes a confidence that the pre-1919 evidence supported.

quote: Of course, Einstein did turn out to be right.
content: The essay's picture is not one decisive test. Its point is that the test was not what located the theory. "Einstein did turn out to be right" concedes nothing to the eclipse, and the note's own account, that GR was "accepted on Mercury's perihelion and on later, better light-deflection measurements," is the essay's. On the plates themselves, a 1979 re-reduction of the Sobral astrographic plates at the Royal Greenwich Observatory, using modern measuring equipment, found them consistent with Einstein's deflection rather than Newton's (Harvey 1979, The Observatory 99). Kennefick's history defends Eddington's handling of the data (Kennefick 2009).

quote: Einstein must have had, already in his possession, sufficient observational evidence to single out the complex equations of General Relativity for his unique attention.
content: The constraints the note calls "mathematical" are compressed observation. The equivalence principle rests on the equality of inertial and gravitational mass, which Eötvös measured to about a part in 108. The Newtonian limit encodes two centuries of celestial mechanics, and energy conservation is the most tested generalization in physics. The Entwurf episode is the essay's arithmetic at work. Those constraints narrowed the field to a small family of candidates; Einstein held the wrong member for two years; and in November 1915 the perihelion of Mercury, which the Entwurf could not account for and the new equations fit exactly, confirmed the switch (Janssen 2005). "Free creations of the human mind" describes how the equations felt to their author, and that is the phenomenon the essay says hunches conceal.

quote: Einstein probably had overwhelmingly more evidence than would, in principle, be required for a perfect Bayesian to assign massive confidence to General Relativity.
content: The essay anticipates this in its fifth sentence: "I try to avoid criticizing people when they are right. If they genuinely deserve criticism, I will not need to wait long for an occasion where they are wrong." The argument is conditional on having located the correct hypothesis: if the brain singled out the needle, it had the bits to be confident. For the unified field theory and the rejection of quantum indeterminism the premise fails, because those hypotheses were not correct, and nothing in the argument licenses confidence in them. Choosing a case in which the antecedent holds is not survivorship bias. It is how a conditional is illustrated.

quote: Suppose General Relativity is a 29.3-bit hypothesis.
content: "Suppose" is doing its ordinary work. The essay's claim is that the evidence needed to reach a given posterior equals the prior improbability in bits, and that a posterior sitting just above one half is unlikely. Both hold for any prior. A simplicity prior raises GR's prior and lowers the number of bits needed, which makes Einstein's confidence easier to justify, not harder. On the essay's accounting, the eliminating work the note assigns to "consistency" is free anyway, because logically inconsistent candidates never had any prior mass to eliminate. The illustrative uniform prior is the worst case, and the argument survives even that.
